input.question: Could every individual proton be called "hydrogen"?
input.ground_truth: In general, a "free" proton (one without an electron, or not bonded to a molecule) is called a proton in Chemistry. There are times when H^+ is a preferred name (pH, etc.), but we do not call *all* individual protons "hydrogen cations". They are fundamentally the same, of course - there is nothing really *wrong* with calling them "hydrogen", but it may be confusing as it is non-standard.

A **hydrogen atom** is like a tiny house, and inside that house is one proton and one electron (imagine a little ball and a little dot).

So, **every proton is NOT always called "hydrogen"**.  
A proton by itself is just a tiny ball.  
But when that proton is inside a hydrogen atom (with its electron friend), then we can call the whole thing "hydrogen".

So,  
- A **proton** is just a part.
- **Hydrogen** is the whole tiny house (proton + electron).

That’s why we can’t call every proton “hydrogen”—it needs its electron friend to be a hydrogen atom!
